find: five of his brothers and sisters died in infancy
replace: five of his brothers died in infancy
note: F1: Chapter 1 records “five little stone lozenges… sacred to the memory of five little brothers of mine” — brothers only.

find: it literally means she breastfed him (hand-rearing), but it also suggests

find: He tells Pip: “We’d be uncommon. We’d go down the river and see the ships.”
replace: He tells Pip: “Ever the best of friends; an’t us, Pip? Don’t cry, old chap!”
note: F3: fabricated Joe quotation — no such line in the novel. Replaced with the genuine Ch. 7 line.

find: Miss Havisham raises Estella to be “proud and hard and beautiful”
replace: Miss Havisham raises Estella to be “proud and hard”
note: F4: ‘proud and hard and beautiful’ is not in the novel. Miss Havisham’s own words (Ch. 38) are ‘proud and hard’.

find: dies in agony, consumed by the fire that engulfs her wedding dress — a symbolic punishment
replace: is badly burned when her wedding dress catches fire, and dies of her injuries weeks later — a symbolic punishment
note: F5: Pip smothers the fire and saves her (Ch. 49); Joe reports she died about a week after Pip fell ill (Ch. 57).

find: He cries in the garden: “I took the opportunity of being alone to use my sleeve to wipe my eyes.”
replace: He hides behind a gate in the brewery-lane: “As I cried, I kicked the wall, and took a hard twist at my hair.”
note: F6: fabricated quotation, welded from two different Ch. 8 sentences. Real wording restored.

find: When he tells the reader he went home and kicked the wall of the forge in frustration
replace: When he tells the reader he hid behind a gate and kicked the brewery wall in frustration
note: F7: Pip kicks the brewery wall at Satis House straight after Estella leaves, not the forge wall at home.

expect: Why does Miss Havisham raise Estella to be 'proud and hard and beautiful'?
value: Why does Miss Havisham raise Estella to be 'proud and hard'?
note: F4: same misquotation on the flashcard prompt.

find: He looks at Joe’s honest, soot-covered face and feels “a growing dissatisfaction” with his home.
replace: Even before the news, a visit to Satis House had left him “dissatisfied with my home and with my trade and with everything.”
note: F8: ‘a growing dissatisfaction’ is not in the novel. Real wording is Ch. 15.

find: He describes Magwitch’s hands as “coarsened and hardened” and physically shrinks from his touch.
replace: He describes Magwitch’s “large brown veinous hands” and admits “the repugnance with which I shrank from him.”
note: F9: ‘coarsened and hardened’ appears nowhere in the novel. Ch. 39 wording restored.

find: Pip’s language of revulsion (‘coarsened,’ ‘hardened,’ shrinking away)
replace: Pip’s language of revulsion (‘abhorrence,’ ‘repugnance,’ ‘I shrank from him’)
note: F9: the exam tip told students to quote words Dickens never wrote.

find: Dickens forces the reader to recognise the hypocrisy: Pip’s money was always criminal money, whether it came from a convict or from Miss Havisham (whose wealth derived from her family’s brewery and Compeyson’s fraud).
replace: Dickens forces the reader to recognise the hypocrisy: Pip earned none of the money himself. Miss Havisham’s fortune came from her father’s brewery, and Compeyson never added to it — he cheated great sums out of her.
note: F10: reversed fact. Herbert (Ch. 22) says Compeyson ‘got great sums of money from her’; her wealth came from her father the brewer.

find: At their trial, Compeyson received a lighter sentence because he “looked like a gentleman” while Magwitch, “in rags and dirt,” was sentenced to fourteen years.
replace: At their trial Magwitch saw “how gentlemanly Compeyson looked, wi’ his curly hair and his black clothes and his white pocket-handkercher, and what a common sort of a wretch I looked.” Compeyson got seven years; Magwitch got fourteen.
note: F11: both quoted phrases are invented. Ch. 42 gives the real wording and the seven/fourteen year split.

find: Yet because he “looked like a gentleman,” the law treated him more leniently.
replace: Yet because he looked and spoke like a gentleman, the law treated him more leniently.
note: F11: quotation marks removed — the phrase is not Dickens’s.

find: In Chapter 44, he tells her: “You let me go on” — accusing her of allowing him to believe she was his benefactor when she knew she was not.
replace: In Chapter 44 he accuses her of letting him believe she was his benefactor. She admits it: “I let you go on.”
note: F12: speaker error. Pip says ‘you led me on?’; ‘I let you go on’ is Miss Havisham’s admission (Ch. 44).

find: Pip, Herbert, and a boatman attempt to smuggle Magwitch out of England
replace: Pip, Herbert, and their friend Startop attempt to smuggle Magwitch out of England
note: F13: Wemmick tells Pip NOT to hire a Thames waterman — ‘Take Startop’ (Ch. 45). Startop rows with them.

expect: What Pip line confronts Miss Havisham about her deception?
value: What does Miss Havisham admit when Pip confronts her about her deception?
note: F12: the line was attributed to the wrong speaker.

value: 'I let you go on' — Miss Havisham's own admission.
note: F12: correct wording and speaker.

expect: Magwitch's gentleman partner — got a lighter sentence because he 'looked like a gentleman.'
value: Magwitch's gentleman partner. He got seven years to Magwitch's fourteen because he looked and spoke like a gentleman.
note: F11: removes the invented quotation and adds the real sentences.

expect: Miss Havisham — he jilted her at the altar.
value: Miss Havisham — he jilted her by letter on her wedding morning, at twenty to nine.
note: F14: she never reached the altar; the letter came while she dressed (Ch. 22).

find: The adult narrator comments with devastating simplicity: “Joe had brought with him a simple dignity.”
replace: Pip’s cry to him says everything: “O Joe, you break my heart! Look angry at me, Joe. Strike me, Joe. Tell me of my ingratitude. Don’t be so good to me!”
note: F15: misquoted and misplaced. Ch. 27 reads ‘there was a simple dignity in him’; the nursing scene is Ch. 57.

find: Pip takes her hand and says: “I saw no shadow of another parting from her.”
replace: Pip takes her hand, and the novel closes: “I saw no shadow of another parting from her.”
note: F16: the line is narration, not speech to Estella.

find: Estella is raised by Miss Havisham as an instrument of revenge — “proud and hard and beautiful.”
replace: Estella is raised by Miss Havisham as an instrument of revenge — “proud and hard.”
note: F4: same invented phrase as Lesson 2.

find: He wants to prove that even a convict can “make” a gentleman: “Own colonist as shall be a gentleman!”
replace: He wants to prove that even a convict can “make” a gentleman: “All on you owns stock and land; which on you owns a brought-up London gentleman?”
note: F17: fabricated Magwitch quotation. Ch. 39 gives the real boast.

expect: Miss Havisham — making her 'proud and hard and beautiful.'
value: Miss Havisham — making her 'proud and hard' so she can break men's hearts.
